deck.title: Budgeting, Finance, and Economic Analysis Concept Cards

cards.backDefinition: The process of estimating the money, people, time, equipment, services, and other resources needed to implement safety and health objectives and translating those needs into planned budget amounts.
cards.whyItMatters: A safety plan cannot be implemented reliably if the required resources are not identified and funded. Budget development links prevention activities to realistic resource needs and organizational planning.
cards.keyPoint: Estimate resource needs early and align the budget with the work required to achieve the safety objective.

sourceRefs.locator: Management Leadership > Allocate resources and integrate safety and health into planning and budgeting processes

cards.backDefinition: A structured forecast of the resources and monetary costs required to complete a defined project, program, acquisition, or intervention over an identified scope and period.
cards.whyItMatters: Reliable cost estimates support realistic planning, budgeting, affordability decisions, and comparison of alternatives before money is committed.
cards.keyPoint: A useful cost estimate is tied to a defined scope, assumptions, schedule, data, and estimating method.

sourceRefs.locator: GAO-20-195G > cost estimating process, scope, schedule, assumptions, data, methods, documentation, and updates

cards.backDefinition: The total cost of an option across its full life, including relevant acquisition, implementation, operation, maintenance, support, and disposal costs rather than only the initial purchase price.
cards.whyItMatters: A low purchase price can hide expensive operation, maintenance, or disposal. Life-cycle cost helps compare alternatives on the basis of their full economic burden.
cards.keyPoint: Compare alternatives using the full cost over the relevant life cycle, not purchase price alone.

sourceRefs.locator: GAO-20-195G > life-cycle cost estimate includes costs across the program life cycle

cards.backDefinition: A cost estimate distributed across the planned schedule or budget periods so decision-makers can see when funds and resources are expected to be needed.
cards.whyItMatters: Total cost alone does not show cash-flow or funding timing. Time phasing connects cost to project milestones, implementation sequence, and budget availability.
cards.keyPoint: Link estimated costs to the schedule so funding is available when the work occurs.

sourceRefs.locator: GAO-20-195G > cost-estimate scope and schedule, program planning, budgeting, and management

cards.backDefinition: A cost view that separates readily attributable expenses, such as medical or workers' compensation costs, from less visible consequences such as replacement training, investigation, lost productivity, repair, absenteeism, and disruption.
cards.whyItMatters: Ignoring indirect costs can materially understate the economic impact of incidents and distort comparisons between prevention investments and the cost of doing nothing.
cards.keyPoint: Include both visible direct costs and credible indirect costs when building the safety business case.

sourceRefs.locator: Business Case for Safety and Health - Costs > direct and indirect workplace injury and illness costs

cards.backDefinition: A financial measure comparing the net economic gain from an investment with the amount invested, commonly expressed as a ratio or percentage to show the return generated relative to cost.
cards.whyItMatters: ROI translates a safety or health investment into business terms that can help decision-makers compare competing uses of limited funds.
cards.keyPoint: Use credible costs and benefits and state the time period and assumptions behind the ROI result.

sourceRefs.locator: Business Case for Safety and Health - Benefits > return on investment and economic benefits of safety and health investments

cards.backDefinition: A structured economic analysis that identifies and values relevant benefits and costs over a defined period, adjusts future values as appropriate, and compares them to determine whether an option's benefits justify its costs.
cards.whyItMatters: Benefit-cost analysis makes assumptions explicit and gives decision-makers a consistent basis for comparing prevention alternatives with different cost and benefit profiles.
cards.keyPoint: Define the baseline, include material benefits and costs, use a consistent time horizon, and discount future values when required.

sourceRefs.locator: OMB Circular A-94 > guidelines for benefit-cost analysis of federal programs

cards.backDefinition: The ratio of the present value of quantified benefits to the present value of quantified costs for an option, used as one indicator of whether measured benefits exceed measured costs.
cards.whyItMatters: The ratio provides a compact comparison of economic value, but it should be interpreted alongside assumptions, scale, uncertainty, and other decision criteria.
cards.keyPoint: A ratio above one means measured benefits exceed measured costs on the stated basis.

sourceRefs.locator: OMB Circular A-94 > benefit-cost analysis using discounted benefits and costs

cards.backDefinition: The present value of benefits minus the present value of costs over the selected analysis period after future amounts are converted to a common present-value basis.
cards.whyItMatters: NPV allows alternatives with costs and benefits occurring at different times to be compared on a consistent monetary basis.
cards.keyPoint: Positive NPV means discounted benefits exceed discounted costs under the stated assumptions.

sourceRefs.locator: OMB Circular A-94 > present-value treatment of benefits and costs

cards.backDefinition: The rate used to convert future monetary benefits or costs into present values so amounts occurring at different times can be compared on a consistent basis.
cards.whyItMatters: The selected discount rate can materially affect long-term economic results, especially when costs occur early and benefits occur many years later.
cards.keyPoint: Use the rate required by the governing analysis framework and test material uncertainty when appropriate.

sourceRefs.locator: OMB Circular A-94 and Appendix C > discount rates for benefit-cost and related analyses

cards.backDefinition: An analysis that compares the costs of alternatives that pursue the same or similar objective when important benefits cannot reasonably be expressed in monetary terms.
cards.whyItMatters: Cost-effectiveness analysis helps identify which option achieves the required safety or health outcome with the least resource use without forcing every benefit into a monetary value.
cards.keyPoint: Use cost-effectiveness when alternatives share a comparable objective but monetizing benefits is not appropriate or practical.

sourceRefs.locator: OMB Circular A-94 > cost-effectiveness analysis guidance

cards.backDefinition: Testing how an economic conclusion changes when important assumptions, cost inputs, benefit estimates, schedules, or other uncertain variables are varied within plausible ranges.
cards.whyItMatters: A result that changes dramatically under small assumption changes is less robust than one that remains stable across credible scenarios.
cards.keyPoint: Identify the assumptions that drive the decision and test how much the result depends on them.

sourceRefs.locator: GAO-20-195G > sensitivity and risk analysis in cost estimating

cards.backDefinition: Early planning for obtaining goods or services that defines the need, involves relevant technical and business disciplines, evaluates alternatives and constraints, and addresses cost, schedule, performance, and life-cycle considerations.
cards.whyItMatters: Early cross-functional involvement allows safety requirements to influence specifications, alternatives, timing, and total cost before procurement decisions become difficult or expensive to change.
cards.keyPoint: Bring safety requirements into procurement planning before solicitation and award decisions are locked in.

sourceRefs.locator: FAR 7.104 and 7.105 > early acquisition planning, multidisciplinary team, cost, schedule, capability, and life-cycle cost

cards.backDefinition: Evaluation of a proposed price without examining its separate cost elements and profit, using appropriate comparisons or other techniques to judge whether the overall price is fair and reasonable.
cards.whyItMatters: Price analysis helps procurement teams assess the reasonableness of an offered price when detailed cost-element analysis is unnecessary or unavailable.
cards.keyPoint: Price analysis evaluates the total proposed price rather than breaking it into individual cost elements.

sourceRefs.locator: FAR 15.404-1 > price analysis and techniques for fair and reasonable pricing

cards.backDefinition: Evaluation of the individual cost elements and profit or fee in a proposal to judge cost reasonableness, cost realism, and what the work should reasonably cost under efficient performance.
cards.whyItMatters: Cost analysis helps identify unsupported, excessive, duplicated, or unrealistic elements that may be hidden within an overall proposed price.
cards.keyPoint: Cost analysis examines the underlying cost elements; price analysis focuses on the overall price.

sourceRefs.locator: FAR 15.404-1 > cost analysis of separate cost elements and profit or fee
